newsitem.title: USA: Clinton ignores Republican attacks on financing.
newsitem.headline: Clinton ignores Republican attacks on financing.

text.p: Ignoring a chorus of Republican criticism of Democratic Party fundraising tactics, President Bill Clinton on Sunday helped raise several million dollars to boost the prospects of Democratic congressional candidates on Nov 5.

Clinton started his labours at a luncheon in Teaneck, New Jersey, to raise money for Representative Robert Torricelli, who is embroiled in a nasty mudslinging fight with Republican Representative Richard Zimmer for the Senate seat vacated by retiring Democrat Bill Bradley.

He then travelled to the Rockefeller family estate in Tarrytown, New York, for a Democratic Senate campaign committee event hosted by West Virginia Sen. Jay Rockefeller, and planned to wind up the day at a fundraising gala in the heart of Manhattan with actress-comedian Whoopi Goldberg.

Asked about Clinton's silence on Republican charges that his party improperly accepted massive contributions from foreign fat cats hoping to buy influence, Clinton campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart said the Democratic National Committee (DNC) was "doing a good job responding to overblown, unsubstantianted, highly partisan Republican attacks."

The DNC is under fire for accepting hundreds of thousands of dollars in questionable campaign contributions from individuals with ties to the Lippo Group, an Indonesian real estate and banking conglomerate.

Clinton, who appears to be well ahead of Republican challenger Bob Dole 16 days before the election, has mentioned the fundraising uproar only once -- in response to a reporter's question at a picture-taking session with Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri on Friday.
He said only that he asked the DNC to review all donations and assure that they were appropriate.

Shortly thereafter, the party organisation announced it had taken away the fund-raising duties of its vice president for finance, John Huang, who formerly worked for the Lippo Group. The DNC also asked the Federal Election Commission to investigate donations he brought in.

Republicans want a broader probe into a matter that Republican House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich says is "the largest scandal to affect the presidency in the history of the United States."

But White House chief of staff Leon Panetta on Sunday dismissed the Republican onslaught as hypocrisy and as a negative tactic that is not working to help Dole. Panetta, interviewed on the NBC News programme "Meet the Press," claimed the Republicans also accepted contributions from foreign backers.
The Boston Globe reported last week that Dole received donations from Jose Fanjul, a wealthy Florida sugar producer who is a Cuban citizen but who holds a Spanish passport.

And Washington's "Roll Call" newspaper reports in a story to appear on Monday that the Republican National Committee returned a $15,000 political donation to a Canadian firm, Methanex, after it learned that the methanol producer had no U.S. operations at the time of the contribution in 1995.
Federal election laws allow foreign citizens who are residents of the United States to make political contributions even though they are not eligible to vote.
